title: Class 5 Maths How Big How Heavy: Volume, Cubes & Weight Explained + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 5 Maths How Big How Heavy: Volume Explained
meta_desc: Class 5 Maths How Big How Heavy made simple: volume in cubic units, how unit cubes fill a box, and its link to weight, with a free quiz and case studies.
excerpt: NCERT Class 5 Chapter 14 asks two honest questions about every object: how big, and how heavy? Here is a plain-English walk through volume in cubic units, why volume survives a change of shape, and its link to weight — with a solved packing case study and a quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Class 5 child an empty matchbox and a shoebox and ask which holds more. They will answer instantly — the shoebox. Then ask how many matchboxes would fill it, and the confident guessing stops. That gap, between knowing something is bigger and being able to say by how much, is exactly what NCERT Class 5 Maths How Big How Heavy (Chapter 14 of Math-Magic) sets out to close. The chapter builds two ideas together: volume, the amount of space a thing takes up, and weight, how heavy that space turns out to be.

I have taught this chapter to Tier 2 city classrooms where the only equipment was a pile of identical erasers, and it still worked. You do not need fancy blocks. You need one repeatable unit and the patience to stack it.

What ‘How Big? How Heavy?’ is really asking

The chapter title is two separate questions wearing one hat. ‘How big’ is about volume — the space inside a box, a brick, or a water tank. ‘How heavy’ is about weight. Children often assume the two rise and fall together, and most of the time they do: a fuller box is usually a heavier box. But the chapter is careful to show where that assumption breaks, and that honesty is what makes it a good chapter rather than a set of formulas.

Measuring volume in cubic units

Volume needs a unit, and the natural unit is a small cube. In NCERT the go-to is a centimetre cube — a little block one centimetre on every side. Its volume is one cubic centimetre, written as cm³. To find the volume of any box, you answer a single question: how many of these unit cubes fit inside with no gaps?

The neat part is that you do not have to fill the whole box to count them. Lay one flat layer along the bottom — say 4 cubes across and 3 cubes deep, so 12 cubes in that layer. If the box is tall enough for 2 such layers, the total is 12 × 2 = 24 cubes, so the volume is 24 cm³. Count a layer, count the layers, multiply. That is the whole method, and it quietly introduces length × breadth × height without ever calling it a formula.

Reading volume straight off a stack

A common exam picture shows cubes stacked in a corner with some hidden behind others. The trick I teach: never count faces, count the box the stack would fill. Find the cubes in the bottom layer, then how many layers high the stack goes, and multiply. Children who count only the cubes they can see always undercount the hidden ones at the back.

Why volume stays the same when the shape changes

Here is the counter-intuitive idea worth slowing down for. Take 12 unit cubes arranged as a flat 4 × 3 tile. Now rebuild them into a tall 2 × 2 × 3 tower. The shape has changed completely — but there are still 12 cubes, so the volume is still 12 cubic units. Rearranging matter does not create or destroy space; it only moves it around.

This is the same reason a lump of dough has the same volume whether you roll it into a ball or flatten it into a roti (its shape changes, not its amount). Once a child truly believes volume is conserved, a whole class of trick questions stops fooling them.

The link between volume and weight

Now the second question — how heavy. If you take the same material, more volume means more weight: two identical bricks weigh twice as much as one. Simple. The twist is that weight also depends on what the thing is made of. A big cardboard box can be lighter than a small iron ball, because iron is packed far more densely than cardboard. So size alone never settles weight; you have to know the material too.

The chapter drives this home with a balance and everyday objects — is a bag of cotton heavier than a stone of the same size? Children love being wrong about this exactly once, and then they remember it.

  • Same material, more volume → more weight.
  • Same volume, different material → weight can differ a lot.
  • Bigger does not automatically mean heavier.
  • Volume is measured in cubic units (cm³); weight in grams and kilograms.

Case study: packing soap boxes

Case-study questions are where the chapter comes alive, so let us solve one properly. A shop packs small soap boxes into a large carton. Each layer holds 5 soap boxes along the length and 4 along the width, and the carton is tall enough for 3 such layers. Each soap box weighs 90 grams.

How many soap boxes fit? One layer holds 5 × 4 = 20 boxes. With 3 layers, that is 20 × 3 = 60 soap boxes.

What does the full carton of soap weigh? 60 boxes × 90 grams = 5400 grams, which is 5.4 kilograms.

The catch question: if the shopkeeper repacks the same 60 boxes into a shorter, wider carton, does the total weight change? No. Same boxes, same material, same count — only the arrangement changed. The volume the soap occupies and its weight both stay the same. That single question tests volume, weight and conservation all at once, which is why case studies matter.

How the two questions compare

QuestionWhat it measuresUnit usedDepends on
How big?Volume — space taken upCubic units (cm³)Length, breadth, height
How heavy?WeightGrams, kilogramsVolume and material
Change the shapeVolume stays the sameCubic unitsOnly the number of cubes

quiz.title: Class 5 How Big How Heavy Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on volume, unit cubes and weight from NCERT Chapter 14. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 5 volume in cubic units and its link to weight

questions.q: A box is filled with unit cubes: 4 along the length, 3 along the width and 2 layers high. How many cubes fit inside?
questions.explanation: One layer holds 4 × 3 = 12 cubes. Two layers give 12 × 2 = 24 cubes, so the volume is 24 cubic units.

questions.q: Which unit is used to measure volume?
questions.explanation: Volume is space in three directions, so it uses cubic units such as the cubic centimetre (cm³).

questions.q: You rebuild 12 unit cubes from a flat tile into a tall tower. What happens to the volume?
questions.explanation: There are still 12 cubes, so the volume is still 12 cubic units. Changing the shape does not change the volume.

questions.q: A cube has a side of 2 cm. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume of a cube is side × side × side = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³.

questions.q: Why can a small iron ball be heavier than a big cardboard box?
options: Weight depends on the material, not just the size
questions.explanation: Weight depends on both volume and what a thing is made of. Iron is packed far more densely than cardboard.

questions.q: One box holds 20 unit cubes and another holds 15. What is the difference in their volumes?
A stack has 6 cubes in its bottom layer and is 3 layers high. How many cubes in all?
questions.explanation: Count a layer, then the layers: 6 × 3 = 18 cubes.

questions.q: A carton holds 5 soap boxes along the length and 4 along the width in one layer, with 2 layers. How many soap boxes fit?
questions.explanation: One layer holds 5 × 4 = 20 boxes. Two layers give 20 × 2 = 40 soap boxes.

faq.q: What is NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 14 ‘How Big? How Heavy?’ about?
faq.a: It teaches volume — the space an object takes up, measured by counting unit cubes in cubic centimetres — and weight, how heavy that object is. It also shows that volume stays the same even when you change an object’s shape.

faq.q: How do you find the volume of a box using unit cubes?
faq.a: Count how many unit cubes fill one flat layer along the bottom, then count how many such layers fit up to the top, and multiply. A box with 12 cubes per layer and 2 layers has a volume of 24 cubic units.

faq.q: Does volume change when an object’s shape changes?
faq.a: No. If you rearrange the same cubes or the same lump of clay into a new shape, the number of cubes — and so the volume — stays exactly the same. Only the shape changes.

faq.q: Is a bigger object always heavier?
faq.a: Not always. Weight depends on the material as well as the size. A large, light object like a cardboard box can weigh less than a small, dense one like an iron ball of the same size.
